Classics Course 17, Class 10 — A Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life, Part One (August 23, 2026)
Video: https://youtu.be/ogW2hu2LO5U?si=LCXVfOI9LFYzebE0
Recap: microdosing emptiness and catching the seed

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: Because there's so much here — and obviously I was realizing that I'm a little bit passionate about it. So where we left off was, we were talking about why we have to continually go for refuge. And by just bringing in what I call microdosing emptiness — you're just dropping in a little bit of emptiness into whatever affliction of the day you're having.

And those afflictions carry us. They really do carry our moods. They carry how we feel, how we feel about ourselves, how we view ourselves — whether we view ourselves as empowered, or whether we view ourselves as disempowered or hopeless. And if you just think of it like microdosing — just put a little bit in, just like a little fairy dust, just a little bit of emptiness. And bit by bit it gets stronger and stronger. And eventually it gets strong enough where it can actually interrupt the affliction. And maybe even stop it.

And so I ended by talking about, what's the name of the game here? Part of it is just saying the same thing over and over again in many, many different ways. Like if A didn't work, then B works, then C works, and then go back to A again. But it's really about, when you have those moments, how do you prevent those seeds from growing? How do you prevent that road rage from turning into some incredibly awful experience? One moment of road rage could turn into six months of just general negativity. Or someone yelling at you all the time. Or worse than that.

And so, how do we — when we finally recognize that we planted a bad seed? That's the first step. You don't even recognize you did it. The speed at which they fly out — you can't even grab them. They're already out. You can't even grab the mental image as it flies out of you. It's too late. And so, recognizing that that seed will grow. But you have to have the recognition first. You have to first recognize it, and catch it. It's an interruption.
Why we practice the four powers constantly

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: And so Shantideva gives us other reasons. Is it just enough to think, oh, I need to interrupt this seed because it's going to continue on and grow into something I don't want? That might not be enough power behind it to offset the flow of your negativity.

But what happens if we don't make efforts in the four powers? What will grow — next slide, Brian — is that we'll continually not understand seeds and their consequences. See, this guy is kind of confused. If we don't continually make efforts, then our misunderstanding of karma and its consequences will grow — like not understanding the connection between things. We'll understand the fake connections and not the real connections. Someone asked me a question at the break, and I said, are those two things connected to each other? And she made a face. And that's what happens when we have a misunderstanding, and we allow the misunderstanding to grow — it just keeps growing.

And so, the reason we would need to do the four forces constantly is: by working on the four powers, it's actually helping us build the understanding of karma and its consequences. Even if we don't know what creates what — even if we're not able to say, well, this creates that — that understanding starts to arise. Like, I know that anger is going to cause something. I know that pride is going to cause it.

Look — when you get good at this, you'll feel the affliction before you put a name on it. Your body will just go, oh. You'll feel it. I'm starting to get tired, so I'm coming up with this — things I only say with my friends sometimes. You know when you're going to have diarrhea? You can feel it. And you know whether it's going to be in two seconds or 15 minutes. Your body feels that and you go, I'm going to have to go to the bathroom soon. Sometimes it's worse than that. But it's the same thing with these negativities. When you start doing things that are going to plant bad seeds, eventually you feel it in your body. You go, oh, that's going to hurt. But that thought of knowing that it's going to plant a negative result is itself planting a seed for you to understand the relationship between the things you do and the results you get.

So it's kind of cool. Thank you, Shantideva. Just doing the four powers helps me understand what seeds to plant when I'm confused. That's the answer to your question. Do the four powers. On what? On everything. It doesn't matter. Just do it constantly. And then that will help ripen the wisdom inside. Next slide.
Closing the gap between listening and doing

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: Doing the four powers also does another thing — it's a different way of saying what I just said: we won't be able to follow even the things we do understand. So the four powers help us purify those seeds, to be able to follow what we do understand. Because look — you can sit in these classes all your life, every single day, and you can listen, listen, listen, listen. You can take notes, you can do all the things. But if you don't have the karma to actually do it — to actually live it is a different karma.

You might have attraction to the ideas. You might be open to the idea — oh, this is the right way to live. I'm really attracted to learning how to be a better person and understanding cause and effect. But there's a gap between listening and doing. And we all struggle with this. I can repeat it till I sleep these ideas. I've dreamed these ideas. But there's a gap between the idea and the action, because we have habits of action from lifetimes that are just on their track. They're just moving. So the four powers start to break that down — that space, that gap between our understanding and our practice. Which I think is another cool moment. Shantideva is pretty damn smart.

Because if any of these things are your problem, he's saying, look, do the four powers and these problems will just resolve. People don't say, I don't know what seed to plant, I'm confused. Well, do four powers on your confusion. And eventually those things will start to soften a little bit. Like if you leave this plastic bottle out in the sun long enough — especially the Arizona sun — it'll start to melt. It's kind of solid right now, but you leave it out there long enough, it'll start smooshing, it'll start taking other shapes. But eventually it'll change enough shape that you'll have an insight. For the time being, before it changes shape, it doesn't feel like anything's changing. And that's also an annoying part of this, because you don't see the foundational changes that are happening until — you shake it up and finally the pressure opens up and it changes.

So we have years and years and lifetimes and countless eons of misunderstandings. So did you think that going to one Dharma class was all of a sudden going to change your life? Well, first of all, A, it did — just not at the speed that you expect it to. But it's the little incremental shifts, and the four powers really can — let me just say that if you do a really good four powers, what comes out on the other side can be absolutely extraordinary. When you really purify something. And that's what I'm going to say about that.

Next, Brian. And finally, the other benefit is that it removes your obstacles to reaching the true wish for enlightenment. It removes the actual obstacles for that. There's the sugarcane version, there's the wish version, and there's the "I want to be a bodhisattva." And then there's the — you finally flush all the crap down, and then you're like, oh, now I feel lighter. Now I get it.
Rejoicing — and the trap of anti-rejoicing

speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
html: Timothy Lowenhaupt: So, rejoicing in good deeds, even the smallest ones — like all of you here, everything you did the last week — you should have a list of a hundred little tiny things that you did, and just use them for your evening meditation, your evening coffee meditation. And we forget. Always forget. And I'm an equal forgetter, so don't think that I'm — again, I have to keep reminding myself. Good night, book club — it's now 10:17, I missed it. But I still will read it a little bit before I go to bed. And if you did do something heavy during the day, definitely do your four powers before going to bed. You don't want that stuff growing overnight.

So, as I said in last class, part of your practice — four powers. Oops. Maybe we should play some Britney Spears. Oops, I did it again. We do it all the time. Oops, I did it again. Yes, I did it again. I do it every five minutes. I do it every 30 seconds. That seed is going to ripen into something bad. Okay, Tim. Has emptiness. Yes. Fine. Then I'm going to try to stop doing that. Now go do something nice. Here, have a chocolate. I purified something a little bit. I did the opposite. I rejoiced in giving away chocolate that landed on the floor. But I tried to do something different.

And Shantideva then says: the problem with you humans is, it's like you do the opposite of rejoicing. And everyone goes, what are you talking about, Shantideva? And he goes, look — you spend all of your time doing the opposite of rejoicing.
